fatal_errors: The hypothesis addresses HfNbTiVAl10 under tensile and fracture testing, whereas the target study designed Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5 within the Nb-Mo-Ta-V-W system and evaluated it primarily by room-temperature compression.
It replaces the target composition-screening method based on rule-of-mixtures modulus, VEC, and density with an unrelated DIC-calibrated finite-element method.
The claimed ±5% modulus/yield accuracy, ±10% toughness accuracy, and 50% computational saving have no cited evidence or derivation.
The proposed benchmark calibrates and evaluates the model against the same experimental campaign, creating circularity unless specimens and outcomes are prospectively held out.
The benchmark is not blinded as requested and provides no independent baseline implementation or predefined runtime-accounting protocol.
Fracture toughness prediction is asserted even though the target evidence concerns compressive fracture strain and does not establish tensile toughness.
explanation: There is only broad thematic alignment in seeking a lower-cost mechanical-property prediction method. The hidden target instead validated composition-based modulus estimates on roughly 130–132 HEAs, screened 38,326 Nb-Mo-Ta-V-W compositions, selected a low-VEC alloy with relatively high modulus, and experimentally demonstrated greatly increased compressive ductility. The generated hypothesis reconstructs neither the alloy, intervention, conditions, mechanism, baseline, nor outcomes. Its DIC–FE concept is generically plausible, and its numerical failure thresholds make it superficially testable, but no supporting evidence is supplied and the validation design lacks blinding and a genuinely held-out prediction set. A decisive benchmark would require preregistered model parameters, unseen specimens or compositions, independent tensile/fracture measurements, blinded scoring, and a fixed comparison against explicitly implemented prior methods.
